strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: efficient initialization of diffusion models at variable model sizes when pre-trained models of the target size are unavailable, which is relevant for real-world deployment across heterogeneous hardware.

The core idea of factorizing weights into layer-shared singular vectors (U, V) and layer-specific singular values (Σ) is a reasonable extension of SVD-based PEFT methods (e.g., SVDiff, KIND) to enable cross-layer knowledge sharing and size-agnostic learngene extraction, which is a sensible technical contribution distinct from prior per-layer SVD approaches.

The paper proposes to extend learngene-style initialization, previously limited to image classification/ViTs, to the more complex domain of diffusion-based image generation, and constructs a benchmark comparing several categories of initialization baselines (direct init, knowledge transfer, learngene-based).

Reported empirical results (Tables 1 and 2) show consistent FID/sFID/IS improvements over compared baselines across several model depths and downstream datasets (CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Bedroom, LSUN-Church), and the method offers claimed savings in training steps and storage relative to training each size from scratch.
weaknesses: Evaluation of 'variable-sized' models is limited to varying depth (L4-L12) at a fixed width (D=1152, as suggested by Figure 2's captions); no experiments vary width or other architectural dimensions, which undercuts the generality claimed by the title and motivation figure about deploying models across diverse hardware/platforms.
Table 1 contains an unresolved placeholder '↓xx.x' in the sFID improvement row for DiT B-L6, indicating incomplete proofreading and reducing confidence in the reported numbers throughout the table.

No ablation studies are provided for key design choices, such as the sharing interval s in Σ, the rank r of the factorization, the number of auxiliary-model training steps (30K), or the amount of downstream data/steps used to optimize Σ during initialization, making it hard to assess sensitivity and justify the specific hyperparameters chosen.

Despite prominently discussing KIND (Xie et al., 2024) as the most closely related SVD-based diffusion method in both abstract-adjacent text and related work, the paper does not include KIND as an experimental baseline, leaving the comparison to the closest prior work incomplete.

No variance/standard deviation is reported despite the Table 1 caption stating n=5 models per method, so it is unclear whether the reported improvements are statistically meaningful given typical run-to-run variability in diffusion training.

The auxiliary-model training stage (30K steps) required to enforce U/V sharing is itself a non-trivial one-time cost that is comparable to the 30K-step baselines (e.g., TLEG, Share Init) it is compared against; while amortized over many downstream sizes, this cost and its overhead relative to baselines requiring the same order of pre-training is not clearly analyzed for a small number of target sizes (e.g., N=1 or 2).

Experiments are restricted to a single backbone/scale (DiT-B) and moderate-resolution datasets (256×256); no experiments at larger diffusion model scale (e.g., DiT-XL or text-to-image models like Stable Diffusion) are shown, limiting evidence that the method scales to the large pre-trained models motivating the introduction.

The writing contains multiple grammatical errors and typos throughout (e.g., 'intialize', 'trainded', 'condenseing', 'pronounces' instead of 'pronounced', 'encodeing'), and some claims (e.g., 'first approach to integrate both size and task considerations') are stated without qualification despite the related work discussing several prior task/size-adaptive learngene methods (WAVE, TLEG) that address parts of this space.

The task-adaptation results (Table 2) use only three downstream datasets, all relatively small and standard in the generative modeling literature (CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Bedroom, LSUN-Church); no more challenging or higher-resolution downstream tasks are tested to establish broader applicability of task-specific Σ adaptation.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and underexplored problem: initializing diffusion models of variable sizes without repeated large-scale pretraining, extending the Learngene paradigm (previously mostly explored for ViT classification) to diffusion transformers for the first time.

The proposed factorization (shared U, V learngenes with layer-specific Σ) is a reasonably clean and intuitive idea that enables lightweight re-adaptation (training only Σ) for new model sizes, avoiding the heuristic layer-selection strategies of prior learngene methods.

Experimental coverage is broad: multiple depths (L4-L12), two backbones (DiT-B/L), six downstream domains (CelebA, LSUN-Bedroom/Church, Hubble, MRI, Pokemon), classification transfer to DeiT-Ti/S, and several ablations (factorization sharing, Σ initialization strategy, PCA visualization of learned Σ).

Consistent, generally sizable improvements over a wide set of baselines (direct init, transfer-based init, learngene-based init) across FID/sFID/IS on most configurations, along with a clear efficiency argument (roughly 3n× speedup versus repeated full pretraining for n target sizes).

The paper includes a useful ablation isolating the benefit of cross-layer weight sharing versus naive per-layer SVD, which helps support the core claim that shared singular vectors carry transferable, size-agnostic knowledge.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly identifies WAVE [11] as the closest prior work (constraint-based pretraining with structural decomposition for scalable initialization) but never includes it as an experimental baseline in any table; similarly, KIND [53], another closely related SVD-based decomposition method, is discussed but not directly benchmarked (only an indirect "w/o Factorize" SVD ablation is provided). This is a significant gap given how central these comparisons are to establishing the paper's incremental contribution over the most relevant recent work.

Despite the title and framing around "variable-sized" models and Figure 2 showing both depth (D) and width (W) variation, essentially all quantitative experiments (Table 1, Table 3) vary only depth; no results are given for width-variable models, which weakens the generality claim implied by the title and abstract.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting is provided for any experiment, despite some reported FID/IS improvements being fairly small (e.g., ~0.1-0.5 for sFID/FID on some settings in Table 2 and Table 1 L6/L8), making it hard to assess statistical robustness of the claimed state-of-the-art results.

Key implementation details affecting reproducibility are missing or under-specified in the main text, such as the rank r used for U/V, sensitivity of results to this rank, and how the pretraining cost per step compares to a standard full-parameter model (the paper reports wall-clock/step-count speedups but not a rigorous accounting of the per-iteration overhead introduced by the factorized reconstruction).

Pretraining is conducted on a single RTX 4090 GPU for 300K steps with batch size 64, which is a relatively small-scale, single-run experimental setup for a diffusion model paper; the largest model tested is DiT-L (231M params), and no results are shown on DiT-XL or larger-scale settings where scalability claims would be more convincing.

The interpretability claims in Section 5.6.3 (PCA visualization suggesting a "linear relationship" and layer correspondence between smaller and larger models) are largely descriptive/qualitative and not rigorously validated beyond visual inspection, echoing similar claims from prior work (TLEG) without deeper analysis of why or when this structure emerges.
